prompt: The bookshop's `pom.xml` names `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` with no `<version>`. Where does its version come from?
hint: Look at the first block of the pom.

choices.text: Maven takes the newest release on Central
choices.why: Maven never picks a version by itself; a dependency with no version and nothing managing it is an error, not a request for the latest.

choices.text: From whatever copy is already in ~/.m2
choices.why: The local repository is a cache of what was downloaded. It answers which files are there, never which version a project should use.

choices.text: From the parent, spring-boot-starter-parent 4.1.1
choices.why: Right. The parent imports spring-boot-dependencies, whose dependency management names a version for every artifact Boot knows, the starters included.

choices.text: A starter has no version of its own
choices.why: It has one, 4.1.1, like every artifact on Central. The pom only leaves it out because the parent supplies it.

prompt: `unzip -l` on `spring-boot-starter-webmvc-4.1.1.jar` lists a manifest, a licence and a notice, and no class. What does the starter contribute, then?
hint: Run `mvn dependency:tree` and look under it.

choices.text: Code that Maven runs while it builds the project
choices.why: Code run during a build comes from plugins, such as spring-boot-maven-plugin. A dependency is put on the classpath and never executed by Maven.

choices.text: Nothing; it is a leftover kept for older projects
choices.why: Swap it for the core starter and Tomcat, Jackson and Spring MVC leave the classpath: the detour's tree went from 39 artifacts to 21.

choices.text: A template that generates the project's first files
choices.why: That is what start.spring.io does, once, before the project exists. A starter is read on every build.

choices.text: Its own dependencies, which arrive with it
choices.why: Right. A starter is a pom whose whole job is its dependency list; the jar is empty because the value is in what it pulls in transitively.

prompt: Which of these did `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` bring into the bookshop with no other line in the pom? Choose all that apply.
hint: The tree in the first section.

choices.text: Tomcat, embedded
choices.why: Right: tomcat-embed-core arrives through spring-boot-starter-tomcat.

choices.text: Jackson, which writes JSON
choices.why: Right: through spring-boot-starter-jackson, at version 3.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL JDBC driver
choices.why: No database is in the tree. A driver is a choice the starter cannot make for you; lesson 9 adds it by name.

choices.text: Logback, behind SLF4J
choices.why: Right: spring-boot-starter-logging comes with every starter, through spring-boot-starter.

choices.text: Hibernate
choices.why: Hibernate belongs to persistence and arrives with spring-boot-starter-data-jpa in lesson 10, not with the web starter.

prompt: A Tomcat security fix ships as 11.0.25 before the next Spring Boot release. What is the change in the bookshop's pom that moves every Tomcat jar to it?
hint: The parent names each library's version in a property.

choices.text: Add <version>11.0.25</version> to spring-boot-starter-webmvc
choices.why: That asks for version 11.0.25 of the starter itself, which does not exist; the starter's version is Boot's, not Tomcat's.

choices.text: Set <tomcat.version>11.0.25</tomcat.version> in <properties>
choices.why: Right. Every Tomcat artifact in spring-boot-dependencies reads that one property, so core, el and websocket all move together.

choices.text: Declare tomcat-embed-core 11.0.25 as a direct dependency
choices.why: That moves one jar and leaves tomcat-embed-el and tomcat-embed-websocket at 11.0.24: a Tomcat assembled from two releases.

choices.text: Delete the copy of Tomcat in ~/.m2 so Maven fetches it again
choices.why: Maven would fetch 11.0.24 again, because that is still the version the build asks for.

prompt: Match each piece of `@SpringBootApplication`, and the call in `main`, to what it does.
hint: Three annotations and one method.

pairs.right: find components in this package and below
build the context and start it

right_distractors: download the libraries the starter names

prompt: A teammate adds a class annotated `@Component` in the package `com.example.reports`. The bookshop starts and never creates it. Why?
hint: Where does the scan start?

choices.text: `@Component` only works together with `@Service`
choices.why: Either annotation alone marks a class as a component; lesson 5 compares them.

choices.text: Components are created lazily, on first use
choices.why: Spring creates singleton beans at start-up by default. This one was never found, so it was never created at all.

choices.text: Its package is not below the main class's package
choices.why: Right. `@ComponentScan` on BookshopApplication scans its own package and the packages below it; `com.example.reports` is a sibling, not a child.

choices.text: The class needs to be listed in application.properties
choices.why: No property lists components. Being under the scanned package is the whole rule.

prompt: `target/` holds `bookshop-0.1.0.jar` at about 19 MB and `bookshop-0.1.0.jar.original` at under 3 kB. What is the difference?
hint: Which plugin ran after the ordinary jar was built?

choices.text: The big one carries every dependency, for `java -jar`
choices.why: Right. spring-boot-maven-plugin's repackage goal put the libraries under BOOT-INF/lib and added a launcher; the .original is what Maven built before that.

choices.text: The big one was compiled with debugging information
choices.why: Debugging information adds bytes to each class, not megabytes to a project with one class.

choices.text: The .original is a backup from the previous build
choices.why: Both are written by the same `mvn package`; nothing in the build keeps the previous one.

choices.text: The big one bundles a JDK, so the server needs no Java
choices.why: Neither contains a JDK; `java -jar` needs Java 25 installed. Putting Java into the artefact is what a container image does, in lesson 23.

prompt: With the bookshop running, `curl -s localhost:8080/` answers a JSON body with `"status":404`. What does that tell you?
hint: Who wrote that JSON?

choices.text: Tomcat failed to start, so curl got an error page
choices.why: A server that failed to start answers nothing at all; curl would report a refused connection.

choices.text: The server works; no code handles `/` yet
choices.why: Right. The request reached Spring MVC, nothing was mapped to `/`, and Boot's default error handling wrote the body. Lesson 6 adds the first controller.

choices.text: The port is wrong; the application listens on 8081
choices.why: Without a profile the bookshop listens on 8080, the default; 8081 comes only with the dev profile.

choices.text: curl needs `-H 'Accept: application/json'` to get a page
choices.why: The answer was already JSON. A header changes the shape of the error, not whether something is mapped to `/`.

prompt: Where does Spring Boot find the list of autoconfiguration classes it considers?
hint: You read one with `unzip -p`.

choices.text: In a central registry Spring downloads at start-up
choices.why: Nothing is downloaded at start-up; the bookshop starts with no network.

choices.text: By scanning every class on the classpath for an annotation
choices.why: That would mean opening thousands of classes on every start. Scanning is for your own package; autoconfiguration is listed.

choices.text: In a file inside each jar, under META-INF/spring
choices.why: Right. Every jar may carry that file, one class name per line, and Boot reads the files of whatever jars are on the classpath.

choices.text: In application.properties, under `spring.autoconfigure`
choices.why: That prefix can exclude a candidate, but the list of candidates comes from the jars, not from your properties.

prompt: The report lists `GsonHttpMessageConvertersConfiguration` under negative matches. What would turn it into a positive match?
hint: Read the reason it printed.

choices.text: Setting `debug=true` in application.properties
choices.why: `debug=true` prints the same report; it changes what you see, never what is decided.

choices.text: Annotating BookshopApplication with `@EnableAutoConfiguration` a second time
choices.why: Autoconfiguration is already on; this candidate was considered and refused for its own reason.

choices.text: Adding a Gson dependency to the pom
choices.why: Right. The condition was `@ConditionalOnClass` on `com.google.gson.Gson`, and a jar on the classpath is the only thing that answers it.

choices.text: Running with `--spring.profiles.active=dev`
choices.why: The dev profile sets a port and a log level; neither puts a class on the classpath.

prompt: In lesson 23 you declare your own `@Bean` of type `ServletWebServerFactory`, configured the way production needs it. What does Boot do with `tomcatServletWebServerFactory`?
hint: Read its condition in the report again.

choices.text: Fails at start-up: two beans of one type
choices.why: There would be only one. The condition exists exactly to avoid that clash.

choices.text: Creates both and lets the last one defined win
choices.why: Spring does not quietly pick one of two beans of the same type to start a server with; Boot's factory is never created.

choices.text: Copies your settings into its own factory
choices.why: Boot's configuration never reads another bean's settings into its own; it either creates its bean or does not.

choices.text: Skips its own, because yours already exists
choices.why: Right. The condition is `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`: Boot's default backs off whenever you supply one, and the report lists it as a negative match.

prompt: To print the conditions evaluation report at start-up, you add one argument: `java -jar target/bookshop-0.1.0.jar --___`.
Which of these did a condition in the bookshop's report check before a configuration was applied? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the parentheses at the end of each line: OnClassCondition, OnBeanCondition…

choices.text: Whether a class is on the classpath
choices.why: Right: `@ConditionalOnClass`, the commonest, as in Gson's negative match.

choices.text: Whether a database answers on its usual port
choices.why: No condition opens a connection. Boot decides from what is installed and configured, before anything is contacted.

choices.text: Whether a property has a given value
choices.why: Right: `@ConditionalOnBooleanProperty`, as in `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled`.

choices.text: Whether a bean of some type is missing
choices.why: Right: `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, which is how a default backs off.

choices.text: How much memory the machine has free
choices.why: Nothing in the report measures the machine; the same jar makes the same decisions on a laptop and on a server.

prompt: A colleague on Spring Boot 3 says the report should show `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` as a negative match. The bookshop's report on Boot 4.1.1 does not mention it at all. Why?
hint: Which jar lists a candidate?

choices.text: Its module's jar is not on the classpath
choices.why: Right. Boot 4 splits autoconfiguration into modules; DataSource's lives in spring-boot-jdbc, which only a JDBC starter brings. A candidate nobody lists is never evaluated.

choices.text: Boot 4 removed DataSource support
choices.why: Lesson 9 configures a DataSource with Boot 4.1.1; the support moved to a module, it did not go away.

choices.text: The report hides configurations with no database
choices.why: The report prints every candidate it evaluated, positive or negative; it filters nothing by subject.

choices.text: `--debug` only shows the configurations that matched
choices.why: The bookshop's own report has a long negative section, Gson's entry among it.

prompt: With only `spring-boot-starter` in the pom, `java -jar` prints `Started BookshopApplication` and the prompt comes back. Why does the process end?
hint: What was keeping it alive before?

choices.text: Spring stops any application that has no controller in it
choices.why: Nothing in Spring checks for controllers. With the web starter and no controller the bookshop kept running, as the first run showed.

choices.text: It crashed after start-up, silently
choices.why: It ended normally: `main` returned and nothing else was left to run. A crash prints an exception and `APPLICATION FAILED TO START`.

choices.text: No web server started, so nothing keeps the JVM alive
choices.why: Right. Tomcat's threads are what kept the JVM alive. Without a web server on the classpath there is no server to start, and the JVM exits when its work is done.

choices.text: The jar was built without spring-boot-maven-plugin's repackage goal
choices.why: The jar ran, and printed Boot's banner and start-up line, so it was an executable jar.

prompt: A nightly job reads a file, writes a report and must exit when done. Which starter suits it best?
hint: What made the detour's application end?

choices.text: spring-boot-starter-webmvc, and call System.exit at the end
choices.why: That starts Tomcat for a job that has no requests to answer, and then has to kill it by hand.

choices.text: spring-boot-starter, the core with no web server
choices.why: Right. The detour showed it: the context starts, the work runs, `main` returns and the JVM exits on its own.

choices.text: No starter; Spring Boot only builds web applications
choices.why: The detour built and ran a Boot application with no web layer at all.

choices.text: spring-boot-starter-tomcat, which is smaller than the web starter
choices.why: That is the web server alone, and its threads would keep the job from exiting.

prompt: The bookshop starts with `--spring.profiles.active=dev`. Which properties files does Boot read?
hint: A profile adds; it does not replace.

choices.text: Only application-dev.properties
choices.why: Then `spring.application.name` would be lost and the log would not say `[bookshop]`; it still does.

choices.text: Only application.properties; profiles are for beans
choices.why: A profile also selects a file, and the port 8081 in the log comes from that file.

choices.text: Both; the dev file wins where they disagree
choices.why: Right. The main file is always read; the profile's file is read on top of it, so its values win and everything else is kept.

choices.text: Every application-*.properties in the jar
choices.why: Only the active profiles' files are read; an application-prod.properties would sit unused.

prompt: Somebody starts the bookshop with `--spring.profiles.active=dve`. What happens?
hint: Is there an application-dve.properties?

choices.text: It runs on 8080 with none of the dev file's settings
choices.why: Right, and the log says so in one line that is easy to miss. A profile with no file is legal, so a typo is never refused: read the profile line after every start.

choices.text: It refuses to start: no such profile
choices.why: Boot has no list of valid profiles to check against; any name is accepted.

choices.text: Boot corrects the name to the closest profile it knows, dev
choices.why: Nothing guesses. The name is used exactly as typed.

choices.text: It starts with no profile at all and logs a warning about it
choices.why: The log reports "dve" as active, at INFO, with no warning; that quietness is the danger.

prompt: Without changing the command line, you choose the dev profile with an environment variable: `___=dev java -jar target/bookshop-0.1.0.jar`.
hint: The property is spring.profiles.active, written the way environment variables are.

prompt: The bookshop is started as `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev SERVER_PORT=9092 java -jar target/bookshop-0.1.0.jar`. On which port does Tomcat start?
hint: The dev file says 8081. Which is stronger, the file or the environment?

prompt: Put these places a setting can come from in order, from the one that wins to the one that loses.
hint: The more deliberate and the later it is given, the stronger.
items: A --server.port=… argument on the command line
server.port in application-dev.properties, with dev active
trap: A file inside the jar is the weakest written source, because it is the one decided before anybody knew where the jar would run.

prompt: Operations start the bookshop with `SERVER_PORT=8443` in a service definition. A developer adds `server.port=8085` to application.properties, rebuilds and deploys. Which port does it use?
hint: Nothing about the environment changed.

choices.text: 8085, because the newer setting wins
choices.why: Precedence is about where a value comes from, not when somebody wrote it; the file is still a weaker source than the environment.

choices.text: 8443; the environment outranks the file
choices.why: Right. The developer's line is read and then hidden by SERVER_PORT. That is the point of the order: a deployment can override a jar without rebuilding it.

choices.text: It fails to start because the two disagree
choices.why: Disagreement is the normal case; Boot resolves it by order and starts with no warning.

choices.text: 8080, because the two cancel each other out
choices.why: Values do not cancel; one source wins and the rest are ignored for that property.

prompt: Why does the environment variable `SERVER_PORT` set the property `server.port` at all?
hint: Shells do not allow a dot in a variable's name.

choices.text: Tomcat reads SERVER_PORT itself, before Spring starts
choices.why: Embedded Tomcat reads nothing from the environment; Boot hands it the port.

choices.text: application.properties maps it with a line you can remove
choices.why: The bookshop's file has no such line; the mapping is a rule, not configuration.

choices.text: It is a special case for the port; other properties need their exact name
choices.why: The same rule turns SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE into spring.profiles.active, as the env var run showed.

choices.text: Boot binds names loosely: upper case, with underscores for dots
choices.why: Right. Relaxed binding reads SERVER_PORT, server.port and --server.port as one property, so each source can spell it the way it is able to.

prompt: Put what happens inside `SpringApplication.run` for the bookshop in the order it happens.
hint: Configuration has to be known before anything is decided from it.
items: The active profiles are settled and their files read
Each autoconfiguration candidate's conditions are evaluated
Tomcat is initialised with the chosen port
trap: The port is a property, so it has to be resolved before Tomcat can be built with it.

prompt: Match each thing you see to what explains it.
hint: Each comes from a different section.

pairs.left: Tomcat started on port 8080 though you asked for dev
The application starts and the prompt returns
pairs.right: no web server on the classpath

pairs.left: A configuration is under negative matches

right_distractors: the JVM ran out of memory

prompt: A staging server must run the same jar with port 8090 and DEBUG logging for `org.springframework.web`, without a rebuild for every change. Which setup fits what this lesson showed?
hint: Which sources can change without touching the jar?

choices.text: Edit application.properties on the server after each deploy
choices.why: That file is inside the jar; editing it means rebuilding, which is what was ruled out.

choices.text: Build a second jar with a staging pom
choices.why: Two jars are two artefacts to test, and the one in staging is no longer the one that ships.

choices.text: Two environment variables in the service definition
choices.why: Right: SERVER_PORT and LOGGING_LEVEL_ORG_SPRINGFRAMEWORK_WEB. Both are ordinary properties, the environment outranks every file in the jar, and changing a variable needs a restart, not a build.

choices.text: Add `@Profile("staging")` to BookshopApplication
choices.why: `@Profile` decides whether a bean exists; it sets no property, and on the main class it would switch the whole application off outside staging.

prompt: Which of these change what the bookshop does WITHOUT running `mvn package` again? Choose all that apply.
hint: What is read when the jar starts, and what was fixed when it was built?

choices.text: Adding `--spring.profiles.active=dev` to the command
choices.why: Right: read at start-up, like every command-line argument.

choices.text: Removing a starter from pom.xml
choices.why: The classpath is decided at build time; the jar keeps every library it was built with until you package again.

choices.text: Setting SERVER_PORT in the environment
choices.why: Right: the environment is read on every start.

choices.text: Changing server.port in src/main/resources/application-dev.properties
choices.why: The jar carries a copy of that file made by the last build; the edit reaches the application only after `mvn package`.

choices.text: Adding `--debug` to the command
choices.why: Right: a command-line argument, so the next start prints the report.
